title: Outsourcing Revenue Cycle Management: What to Consider
summary: Learn what RCM workflow to outsource and how full, selective, and AI-led outsourcing models compare, and how to evaluate vendors and measure ROI.
body_markdown:
> Revenue cycle management outsourcing moves some or all revenue cycle work — eligibility, coding, claim submission, A/R follow-up, denials, and appeals — to an external vendor that supplies people, software, or both. There are three models: full outsourcing (the whole cycle), selective outsourcing (specific functions like A/R or coding), and AI-led models that automate repeatable work and connect the cycle so downstream denial patterns improve upstream coding.
>
>
> CombineHealth is a[self-learning autonomous healthcare RCM platform](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/healthcare-revenue-cycle-management-software-companies) built for the AI-led model: it can replace selected manual workflows, add an assurance layer over your existing team or vendor, or connect eligibility through appeals end to end.


> **Key Takeaways**
>
>
> • RCM outsourcing transfers some or all revenue cycle work to a service provider that supplies people, software, or both. A/R follow-up, coding, and denials management are the most commonly outsourced functions.
>
>
> • Measure any RCM outsourcing model by outcomes such as denial rate, days in A/R, and cost to collect.
>
>
> • Selective RCM outsourcing suits most organizations with an existing team, while full outsourcing suits those without internal RCM capability.
>
>
> • Score each RCM workflow, then automate, outsource, retain, or run it as a hybrid. AI-led models handle repeatable work and route uncertain cases to human reviewers.
>
>
> • CombineHealth is one of the leading RCM AI platforms. It can replace manual workflows, support internal or outsourced teams, or connect eligibility, coding, denials, and appeals in one end-to-end model.


Sixty-nine percent of healthcare organizations outsource all or part of their revenue cycle, according to the[2026 Guidehouse and HFMA RCM Trends survey](https://guidehouse.com/insights/healthcare/2026/rev-cycle-trends-report) . Outsourcing is no longer the exception. The harder question is what you outsource and how it gets done.


You can outsource the entire revenue cycle, outsource selected functions, or use AI software to automate repeatable work while internal or external specialists handle exceptions.


This guide explains how to choose between them, what to ask vendors, and how to measure the return.

## What Is Revenue Cycle Management Outsourcing?


Revenue cycle management (RCM) outsourcing is the **practice of transferring some or all revenue cycle work, from eligibility checks through medical claim payment and appeals, to an external RCM vendor.** Healthcare organizations use it to add capacity, payer knowledge, or technology they lack internally. The vendor may supply people, software, managed services, or all three.


- A labor-based vendor assigns trained billers and coders to work inside your systems.
- A technology-enabled vendor adds automation to the same workflows.
- An AI-led model completes high-volume tasks with software and routes only uncertain cases to human reviewers.


Whatever the[RCM outsourcing](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/healthcare-revenue-cycle-management) model, measure the result with metrics such as denial rate and days in A/R.


## Which Revenue Cycle Functions Can Be Outsourced?


Nearly every revenue cycle function, from eligibility verification to appeals, can be outsourced, but organizations rarely outsource all of them. A[Guidehouse and HFMA survey](https://guidehouse.com/insights/healthcare/2026/rev-cycle-trends-report) found that 67% outsource A/R follow-up and collections, 50% use outsourced coders, 39% outsource denials management, and 29% outsource billing and claims editing.


The pattern suggests that leaders tend to outsource back-end functions where internal teams face capacity constraints. Back-end workflows generally follow clearer rules and involve fewer patient-facing touchpoints, making them a lower-risk starting point for outsourcing.

## Why Do Healthcare Organizations Outsource RCM?


Healthcare organizations outsource RCM to add capacity and specialized expertise faster than internal hiring allows. RCM outsourcing also helps cover hard-to-staff functions, such as payer follow-up and appeals, without building the same team in-house. The strongest engagements tie each benefit to a measurable outcome.


These benefits are most useful when they can be tied to a measurable outcome:


- **Relief from staffing shortages and turnover:** vacancy days and A/R backlog size.
- **Specialized coding and payer knowledge:** coding accuracy and first-pass acceptance rate.
- **Extended operating coverage:** claims worked per day.
- **Scalability during volume changes:** backlog size during volume spikes.
- **Lower recruiting and training burden:** cost per hire and time to productivity.
- **Faster claim submission:** days from discharge to billed.
- **More consistent payer follow-up:** days in A/R.
- **Greater denial-management capacity:** denial rate and overturn rate.
- **Access to automation and analytics:** cost to collect.
- **More predictable operating costs:** variable fees versus fixed payroll.


## Full RCM Outsourcing or Selective Outsourcing: Which Is Better?


Selective outsourcing is the better fit for organizations with a working internal team and specific bottlenecks. Full outsourcing fits organizations without internal RCM leadership or the systems needed to manage the revenue cycle. Selective models keep more visibility in-house and let organizations change vendors function by function. Full models simplify management but make it harder to bring workflows back in-house or switch vendors later.

## How Is AI Changing RCM Outsourcing?


AI changes RCM outsourcing by changing how the work gets done, not just who does it.


Traditional outsourcing moves a manual workflow to an external team. Technology-enabled outsourcing gives that team automation tools, while AI-led models use software to complete repeatable tasks. McKinsey estimates that[AI enablement could cut cost to collect by 30% to 60%](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/healthcare/our-insights/agentic-ai-and-the-race-to-a-touchless-revenue-cycle) .


The larger shift is connection. When[eligibility](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/best-medical-insurance-eligibility-verification-software) , coding, claim validation, A/R follow-up, denial management, appeals, and analytics share one decision record, a denial pattern found downstream can change coding and claim-validation rules upstream. Separate vendors for each step rarely close that loop.

Eligibility, coding, claim validation, A/R, denials, appeals, and analytics share one decision record, and its[payer intelligence](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/payer-intelligence-ai-medical-coding) learns from real claim outcomes — denials, reimbursements, underpayments — so patterns found downstream feed back into upstream coding and claim-validation rules. That closed loop is the thing separate single-function vendors can't replicate, and it's where AI-led RCM pulls ahead of simply moving manual work to an external team.


## Should You Outsource RCM or Use RCM Automation Software?


**Outsource RCM when the bottleneck is capacity or specialized expertise, and buy RCM automation software when the bottleneck is repeatable, rules-driven work your team already understands** . Outsourcing adds people, but software reduces the number of people the work requires.


You can use this as a starting rule:


- **Capacity problem, standard work:** automation software or an AI-led service.
- **Expertise problem, complex work:** a specialized vendor, with software handling the routine volume.
- **Visibility problem:** an audit layer that works across your existing vendors.


> CombineHealth gives you a third option that blends both. It automates the high-volume, rules-driven work — eligibility, coding, claim validation — so the work needs fewer people, and for the visibility problem, it can run as an audit layer across your existing vendors, checking their coding quality, claim errors, and denial root causes without ripping out what you have. You can start with one bottleneck or connect the full cycle.


## How Should You Decide What to Outsource?


Score each RCM workflow, then assign it to one of four models: automate, outsource, retain, or hybrid. The score matters more than the vendor pitch, because it shows where the work is actually expensive, error-prone, or hard to staff. Run the exercise per workflow, such as eligibility verification, coding, or[appeals](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/top-denial-appeal-platforms) , not for the revenue cycle as a whole.


Score every workflow on:


- **Volume and manual effort:** how many transactions, and how many touches each.
- **Error and denial impact:** how often the work fails, and what it costs when it does.
- **Financial value:** how much revenue depends on the workflow.
- **Rule consistency and clinical complexity:** whether payer and coding rules are stable, and how much clinical judgment is needed.
- **Staffing difficulty and specialty expertise:** how hard the role is to hire and train for.
- **Patient-facing needs and integration readiness:** whether patients interact with it, and whether your[EHR and clearinghouse connections](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/autonomous-medical-coding-platforms-ehr-integration) are ready.


Then assign each workflow:


- **Automate:** high-volume, repeatable, rules-driven work, such as eligibility verification and claim validation.
- **Outsource:** specialized or capacity-constrained work with measurable service-level agreements (SLAs), such as aged A/R.
- **Retain internally:** strategic, patient-facing, contractual, or high-judgment decisions, such as payer contract strategy.
- **Hybrid:** work that is mostly automatable but produces comp lex exceptions, such as coding and appeals.


## How Should You Evaluate an RCM Outsourcing Company?


Evaluate an RCM outsourcing company on what it will prove, not what it promises: automation rates, exception handling, reporting transparency, and exit terms. Use the scorecard below in every vendor conversation.


**Evaluation area**


**Ask the vendor**


**Warning sign**


Scope and specialty

Experience limited to a different care setting


Connectivity


Which EHRs, practice management systems, clearinghouses, and payers do you integrate with?


Manual file transfers as the default


Automation


What share of claims, codes, or follow-ups is processed autonomously versus manually?


No number, or a number without a definition


Medical coding and compliance


What controls and audit trails support coding decisions?


Black-box coding with no rationale


Exception model


How are uncertain cases flagged and resolved?


No documented review process


[Denial prevention](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-medical-coding-denial-prevention)


What do you catch before claims are submitted?


Appeals only


Reporting


Can I see decisions, denials, turnaround time, and cost to collect by payer?


Monthly summaries only


Security and contracts


Will you sign a business associate agreement (BAA)? What are the SLAs, termination terms, and data-return provisions?


Vague exit or data-return language


HIPAA treats a billing or claims-processing vendor as a business associate, which means you need a signed BAA before the vendor handles protected health information. The[HHS guidance on business associates](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr/privacy/hipaa/understanding/coveredentities/businessassociates.pdf) explains the requirement. Ask for customer references too.


## How Do You Measure the ROI of Outsourced RCM?


Measure RCM outsourcing ROI as **financial improvement plus avoided internal cost, minus vendor, integration, and transition costs.** Payroll savings alone understate the value and can hide losses elsewhere, such as higher denial rates. An[RCM vendor](https://www.combinehealth.ai/blog/ai-tools-for-revenue-cycle-management) that costs less than your team but collects less is a net loss.


**RCM outsourcing ROI = financial improvement + avoided internal cost − vendor, integration, and transition costs**


- **Financial improvement:** higher net collections, lower denial write-offs, and fewer days in A/R.
- **Avoided internal cost:** salaries, benefits, recruiting, training, and software you no longer pay for.
- **Costs against the return:** vendor fees, integration work, and the transition period when both teams may run in parallel.

## Take the Next Step With Your Revenue Cycle


Every revenue cycle has work that software can handle, work that needs a specialist, and work your team should keep. Score each workflow on volume, error rate, denial impact, and the judgment it requires. Then assign it to automation, a vendor, your internal team, or a hybrid with exception review.


Start with the one workflow where capacity or expertise is thinnest. Set a baseline for denial rate and days in A/R, and expand once those numbers move. Whichever model you choose, write visibility into denials and coding decisions into the contract.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How does CombineHealth fit into an RCM outsourcing decision?


Three ways: replace a selected manual workflow (like eligibility, coding, or A/R follow-up); augment an internal team or existing RCM vendor as an assurance layer; or connect the full cycle from eligibility through appeals. Most organizations start with the one workflow where capacity or expertise is thinnest, then expand once denial rate and days in A/R improve.


### Can CombineHealth work alongside our existing RCM vendor?


Yes. CombineHealth can run as an assurance layer over your current team or vendor — auditing codes from providers, coders, EHRs, or billing vendors; flagging undercoding and documentation gaps; validating claims before submission; prioritizing A/R and denial work; and comparing performance across payers and providers. You get direct visibility into coding quality and denial root causes without replacing what you already have.


### Does CombineHealth replace our RCM team?


It changes what the team spends time on rather than simply replacing it. CombineHealth autonomously handles the high-volume, repeatable work so staff focus on complex cases, audits, payer strategy, and exceptions — and throughput stops depending on headcount. You can keep your team and add CombineHealth as an automation and assurance layer, or move whole functions to it.


### How does CombineHealth connect the revenue cycle end to end?


CombineHealth connects eligibility, coding and CDI, claim validation and submission, A/R follow-up, denial management, appeals, and analytics in one platform. Its payer intelligence learns from denials, reimbursements, and underpayments, so outcomes from downstream workflows inform upstream prevention — a closed loop that separate single-function vendors rarely achieve.


### How is RCM outsourcing priced?


Pricing varies by vendor and may be a percentage of collections, a flat fee, a per-claim rate, or a custom arrangement. Always compare cost against measurable outcome.


### Is RCM outsourcing HIPAA compliant?


It can be, if the RCM vendor signs a business associate agreement and maintains safeguards for protected health information. Confirm security controls, subcontractor agreements, and data-return terms before signing.


### Can I outsource only part of my revenue cycle?


Yes. Selective RCM workflow outsourcing is common, and most organizations start with one function, such as A/R follow-up or medical coding.


### Can AI replace my current RCM vendor?


Sometimes, for high-volume repeatable work. But many organizations instead layer AI on top of an existing vendor to audit performance and automate routine tasks while medical billing specialists handle exceptions.
